newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Renault to defer Belgian shutdown-paper.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Renault to defer Belgian shutdown-paper.

text.p: Carmaker Renault will defer controversial plans to close its Belgian plant and appoint an independent expert to examine alternatives, the French newspaper Le Monde said on Tuesday.

The report followed a meeting between new French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene on Saturday to discuss the fate of the plant, which still employs around 2,900 after some staff left.

A spokeswoman for Renault, which is owned 46 percent by the state, refused to confirm or deny the report, but sources at the company said an announcement would be made at or after the annual general meeting beginning at 1500 GMT.
The closure planned for July 31 has become a widely watched test of the new left-wing government's industrial policy.
Finance Minister Dominique Stauss-Kahn said on Monday he expected "some positive and interesting developments" for the Vilvoorde workers to be announced on Tuesday.
During last month's general election campaign, the French Socialists pledged they would push Renault to explore alternatives to the plant shutdown.

Le Monde said an expert would study options such as cutting working hours, proposed by trade unions, and reducing costs to save the plant and report back within a month. The Renault board would then decide whether to go ahead with the closure.
It quoted a Renault executive as saying two experts had refused the task because they knew they would reach the same conclusion as the company -- that the closure was inevitable.
Renault, which lost 5.25 billion francs ($909.3 million) last year, has insisted the plant must close to streamline its money-losing car assembly operations and cut costs.
It has already said shorter work weeks are not a solution to Renault's need to bring its scattered production operations in line with those of its competitors in Europe.
Renault says its annual production per site averages 125,000 cars compared with more than 200,000 at Ford, GM Opel and Volkswagen.
French daily Le Figaro, quoting trade union sources, said the Vilvoorde plant closure would be postponed by six months but would ultimately go ahead.
Renault initially set a July 31 deadline but has said that could be extended a few weeks or months.
The weekly newsletter La Lettre de l'Expansion said chairman Louis Schweitzer would offer to promote industrial activities in the Vilvoorde area to employ workers hit by the closure.
Car analysts say they believe the new government would concede, after examining the situation, that tough measures were essential to save Renault.

Dehaene also hinted on Saturday as he left the meeting with Jospin that the new prime minister saw the matter differently now he was in power from the way he had seen it as Socialist opposition leader.
Renault-Vilvoorde workers, who staged a long occupation of the plant after the closure was announced, began another three-day strike on Monday. ($ = 5.773 French Francs)
